characterization_methods.key_findings: For the annealed specimen E the elastic modulus remained almost the same until yielding – the only species for which this holds; curve E stays near 200 GPa before dropping (Fig. 4). Elastic modulus values for E: 224 (0–0.05% strain) and 206 (whole elastic range), the highest among species A–E.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: stress–strain curve measured up to 1% strain; elastic modulus obtained from the stress–strain curve within the elastic deformation region
characterization_methods.purpose: measure the stress–strain curves and obtain the elastic modulus of specimens A–E, including the annealed specimen E, for comparison of the effect of movable dislocations
characterization_methods.technique: tensile test with load cell and strain gauge

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Triboscope nano-indentation instrument (Hysitron Inc.) mounted on an AFM stage (SPM-9500J2, Shimadzu Co.); 3D piezo actuator; force 1–10 mN, 100 nN sensitivity; displacement 5 μm, 0.2 nm sensitivity
characterization_methods.key_findings: The elastic modulus near the grain boundary is smaller than in other regions; confirms that the modulus decrease is localized at grain boundaries. NOTE: the marker-location figure for this indentation is labelled 'SPCE', whereas specimen E belongs to the SPCC material, so these nano-indentation results may belong to a different (SPCE) specimen and are reported here only as the technique used in the study.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: spherical tip (nominal R = 50 μm; also R = 200 μm) used to keep surface deformation elastic; CMP-treated surface; measurement points along lines across a grain boundary at ~1 μm interval
characterization_methods.purpose: measure the distribution of elastic modulus (and hardness) within a grain and near grain boundaries to link microscopic properties to the macroscopic modulus change
characterization_methods.technique: nano-indentation with a spherical indenter tip

defect_interactions.interaction_type: dislocation pile-up at the grain boundary
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Dislocations released from a common source move along the same slip surface and easily pile up, their front being stopped by obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes; the pile-up dislocations can move backwards when the shear stress is released during unloading, which can lower the apparent elastic modulus. The pile-up model (Fig. 3) shows dislocations driven by shear stress tau piling up against a grain boundary.

interfaces.interface_notes: This pile-up/grain-boundary description is the general micro-mechanism invoked by the paper to explain the strain-induced decrease of the apparent elastic modulus.
interfaces.slip_behavior: Dislocations move along the same slip surface and pile up against obstacles (grain boundaries, solutes); pile-up dislocations can move backwards when shear stress is released.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Specimen species E in Table 1 is listed as 'Annealed'. The paper does not report the annealing temperature, time or any other parameter for this condition; the alloy is a 1.2 mm thick SPCC sheet.

No unit for the elastic modulus is printed in Table 2. The stress–strain curve was measured with a load cell and a strain gauge up to 1% strain.

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Fig. 4(a) shows the stress–strain curves of specimens A–E measured by strain gauge up to 0.3% strain; Fig. 4(b) shows the apparent elastic modulus versus strain with curve E staying near 200 GPa before dropping.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Elastic modulus of the annealed specimen E calculated from the whole elastic region of the stress–strain curve. No unit for the elastic modulus is printed in Table 2.

structures.overall_structure: Polycrystalline mild-steel (SPCC) sheet in the annealed condition; dislocations in the Fe matrix are locked by carbon and other solutes (Cottrell effect) before plastic deformation, and the material consists of grains separated by grain boundaries.

unmapped_findings: For specimen E (annealed) the apparent elastic modulus remained almost constant until yielding – it is the only species among A–E for which this is the case; the as-received and pre-strained specimens showed a modulus that decreased from the very beginning of loading (b0032, b0026, b0030).

Among species A–E, the annealed specimen E had the highest elastic modulus: 224 (strain region 0–0.05%) and 206 (whole elastic range), against 182/173 for A, 188/162 for B, 186/162 for C and 189/189 for D; no units are printed in Table 2 (b0034).
The annealing temperature and time (and any other annealing parameter) for specimen E are not reported in the paper (b0027, b0028, b0029).

The paper's precision-extensometer large-deformation tensile test (Section 2) and the V-bending spring-back FEM simulation were performed on SPCE sheet metal, whereas specimen E belongs to the SPCC material of Table 1; those SPCE-specific results are therefore not attributed to this sample (b0013, b0015, b0017, figure_002).
